source_text: Οὐκ ἂν δὲ οὐδὲ ἐφονευόμεθα οὐδὲ δυνατώτεροι ἡμῶν ἦσαν οἵ τε ἄδικοι ἄνθρωποι καὶ δαίμονες, εἰ μὴ πάντως παντὶ γεννωμένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ θανεῖν ὠφείλετο· ὅθεν καὶ τὸ ὄφλημα ἀποδιδόντες εὐχαριστοῦμεν. Καίτοι γε καὶ τὸ ξενοφώντειον ἐκεῖνο νῦν πρός τε Κρίσκεντα καὶ τοὺς ὁμοίως αὐτῷ ἀφραίνοντας καλὸν καὶ εὔκαιρον εἰπεῖν ἡγούμεθα. Τὸν Ἡρακλέα ἐπὶ τρίοδόν τινα ἔφη ὁ Ξενοφῶν βαδίζοντα εὑρεῖν τήν τε ἀρετὴν καὶ τὴν κακίαν, ἐν γυναικῶν μορφαῖς φαινομένας. Καὶ τὴν μὲν κακίαν, ἁβρᾷ ἐσθῆτι καὶ ἐρωτοπεποιημένῳ καὶ ἀνθοῦντι ἐκ τῶν τοιούτων προσώπῳ, θελκτικήν τε εὐθὺς πρὸς τὰς ὄψεις οὖσαν, εἰπεῖν πρὸς τὸν Ἡρακλέα ὅτι, ἢν αὐτῇ ἕπηται, ἡδόμενόν τε καὶ κεκοσμημένον τῷ λαμπροτάτῳ καὶ ὁμοίῳ τῷ περὶ αὐτὴν κόσμῳ διαιτήσειν ἀεὶ ποιήσει. Καὶ τὴν ἀρετὴν ἐν αὐχμηρῷ μὲν τῷ προσώπῳ καὶ τῇ περιβολῇ οὖσαν εἰπεῖν· Ἀλλ᾿ ἢν ἐμοὶ πείθῃ, οὐ κόσμῳ οὐδὲ κάλλει τῷ ῥέοντι καὶ φθειρομένῳ ἑαυτὸν κοσμήσεις ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀϊδίοις καὶ καλοῖς κόσμοις. Καὶ πάνθ᾿ ὁντινοῦν πεπείσμεθα, φεύγοντα τὰ δοκοῦντα καλά, τὰ δὲ νομιζόμενα σκληρὰ καὶ ἄλογα μετερχόμενον, εὐδαιμονίαν ἐκδέχεσθαι. Ἡ γὰρ κακία, πρόβλημα ἑαυτῆς τῶν πράξεων τὰ προσόντα τῇ ἀρετῇ καὶ ὄντως ὄντα καλὰ διὰ μιμήσεως ἀφθάρτων περιβαλλομένη (ἄφθαρτον γὰρ οὐδὲν ἔχει οὐδὲ ποιῆσαι δύναται), δουλαγωγεῖ τοὺς χαμαιπετεῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων, τὰ προσόντα αὐτῇ φαῦλα τῇ ἀρετῇ περιθεῖσα. Οἱ δὲ νενοηκότες τὰ προσόντα τῷ ὄντι καλὰ καὶ ἄφθαρτοι τῇ ἀρετῇ· ὃ καὶ περὶ Χριστιανῶν καὶ τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄθλου καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τῶν τοιαῦτα πραξάντων, ὁποῖα ἔφασαν οἱ ποιηταὶ περὶ τῶν νομιζομένων θεῶν, ὑπολαβεῖν δεῖ πάντα νουνεχῆ, ἐκ τοῦ καὶ τοῦ φευκτοῦ καταφρονεῖν ἡμᾶς θανάτου λογισμὸν ἕλκοντα.
orientation: Justin is explaining why Christians do not fear death, arguing that death is a debt owed by every human, and he turns to Xenophon's story of Heracles at the crossroads to contrast vice and virtue.
pass_a_gloss: And we would not be murdered, nor would the unjust humans and demons be stronger than us, unless death were owed in every way to every human being that is born; whence also, paying the debt, we give thanks. And yet indeed we consider that famous Xenophontic saying now to be good and timely to say both against Crescens and against those who are foolish like him. Xenophon said that Heracles, walking to some crossroads, found both virtue and vice, appearing in the forms of women. And vice, in delicate clothing and with a face made lovely and blooming from such things, being charming immediately to the eyes, said to Heracles that, if he follows her, she will make him live always in pleasure and adorned with the brightest adornment and with adornment like the adornment around her. And virtue, being in a squalid face and in squalid clothing, said: But if you obey me, you will adorn yourself not with adornment nor with beauty that flows and decays, but with the eternal and beautiful adornments. And we are persuaded that every single person, fleeing the things that seem beautiful, and pursuing the things considered hard and irrational, receives happiness. For vice, as a screen for herself of her deeds, clothing herself through imitation of incorruptible things with the things that belong to virtue and are truly beautiful (for she has nothing incorruptible nor can she make anything), enslaves the earth-bound among humans, having put around virtue the base things that belong to herself. But those who have understood the things that belong to what is truly beautiful are also incorruptible in virtue; which thing also concerning Christians and those from the contest and the humans who did such things as the poets said about the so-called gods, every sensible person must suppose, from the fact that we despise even death that is to be fled, drawing a reckoning.

Preserves the participle 'drawing' and the noun 'reckoning', showing the inference drawn from Christians' contempt of death.

pass_b_english: We would not be put to death, and neither unjust people nor demons would be stronger than we are, unless death were absolutely owed by every human being who is born. Therefore, as we pay this debt, we give thanks.
And indeed we think it is good and timely now to say that famous saying of Xenophon to Crescens and to those who are as foolish as he is.
Xenophon said that Heracles, walking along a certain crossroads, found virtue and vice appearing in the forms of women.

Vice, with her delicate clothing and a face made lovely and blooming by such adornment, was immediately charming to the eyes, and she said to Heracles that if he followed her, she would make him live always in pleasure and adorned with the most brilliant adornment, like the adornment around herself.
And virtue, with a squalid face and clothing, said: "But if you obey me, you will adorn yourself not with adornment or beauty that flows away and decays, but with eternal and beautiful adornments."
And we are persuaded that everyone who flees the things that seem beautiful and pursues the things considered harsh and irrational is destined for happiness.

For vice, to screen her deeds, clothes herself by imitating the incorruptible things that belong to virtue and are truly beautiful (for she has nothing incorruptible, nor can she produce anything), and she enslaves the earth-bound among humans, putting her own worthless things upon virtue.
But those who have understood the things that belong to what is truly beautiful are also incorruptible through virtue.

This is what every sensible person must suppose about Christians, about those who strive in virtue's contest, and about the people who did such things as the poets said about the so-called gods, drawing this inference from the fact that we despise even death, which is to be fled.

problems.why: The Greek calls for a discerning mind and despising both hidden and apparent, not merely despising death; key phrase νουνεχῆ is omitted.
problems.fix: one must suppose everything with a discerning mind, despising both the hidden and the apparent, the reasoning of death that draws us

problems.quote: drawing a reckoning from the fact that we despise even a death that is to be fled

problems.why: λογισμὸν ἕλκοντα goes with the subject (sensible person), not 'we'; they draw this inference from our despising death
problems.fix: must draw this inference from our despising even a death that should be fled
problems.ruling: Greek λογισμὸν ἕλκοντα ties to “πρέπει…καταφρονεῖν ἡμᾶς”, not “we”; English misassigns subject and meaning.
